overview: The Guston–Robinson entry represents adjoining major mine workings in the Red Mountain district, not proof that every Guston and Robinson claim or opening was always one legal property.
Development accelerated during the 1882 Red Mountain boom associated with John Robinson and his partners, and the mines helped support the nearby Guston camp.

timeline.text: Development accelerated during the 1882 Red Mountain boom associated with John Robinson and his partners, and the mines helped support the nearby Guston camp.

USGS Bulletin 182 provides a contemporary technical and mapping anchor for the district, while a USGS photograph dated September 14, 1900 records the Robinson, Guston, and Yankee Girl mine landscape together.
The 1893 silver collapse curtailed operations, and early-twentieth-century work sought to drain and reach adjoining mines at depth through the Joker Tunnel.
A period-reported 1885 production value is not treated as an audited lifetime total, and no aggregate total is adopted.
Sources: USGS Bulletin 182, A Report on the Economic Geology of the Silverton Quadrangle (1901); Fort Lewis College Red Mountain Project; USGS 1900 Guston mine-landscape photograph record.

moreHistory: USGS Bulletin 182 provides a contemporary technical and mapping anchor for the district, while a USGS photograph dated September 14, 1900 records the Robinson, Guston, and Yankee Girl mine landscape together.
Historic production centered on silver- and lead-bearing ore, with gold and copper also associated with later district activity.
The 1893 silver collapse curtailed operations, and early-twentieth-century work sought to drain and reach adjoining mines at depth through the Joker Tunnel.
Surviving identification features include large dumps, mine-building ruins, structural remnants, and the steep disturbed mining landscape above Guston.
Component safeguard: keep the Guston and Robinson workings, Guston townsite, Yankee Girl, Orphan Boy, the Joker Tunnel, and later Idarado connections as separate linked elements.
